outcome: No mathematical progress on Polignac's conjecture itself (that every even n is a de Polignac number, i.e. a gap occurring infinitely often) has occurred since 26 January 2024. The best bound remains the Polymath8b [2,246] result from 2014. The only relevant post-window event is an AI-assisted Lean 4 formalization (verification, not new mathematics) of that pre-existing 2014 result, published by the startup Axiom Math on 17 August 2026.

ai.basis_quote: Axiom Math's AxiomProver system has produced a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the strongest known result on gaps between prime numbers... Researchers first wrote the proof as a blueprint with every definition, lemma, and theorem given a label, a precise statement, and a list of the results it depends on. AxiomProver then generated machine-checkable Lean 4 proofs built on Mathlib.

summary: Polignac's conjecture (every positive even n is a de Polignac number, occurring as a prime gap infinitely often) remains fully open since the frozen revision. The best known partial result is still Polymath8b's 2014 demonstration that at least one even number in [2,246] is a de Polignac number (following Zhang 2013 and Maynard 2013) — this predates the window and is unchanged. Searches for post-window mathematical progress (new bounds, new cases settled, a full proof, or a disproof) turned up nothing: two 2024 papers (Banks, 'Consecutive primes and IP sets', arXiv:2403.10637, March 2024; Goswami, 'An Explicit Ramsey Bound for de Polignac Numbers', arXiv:2406.02243, June 2024) study Ramsey/IP-set structural properties of the *set* of already-known de Polignac numbers, but neither extends the range of proven gaps, settles a new case, or touches the general conjecture — they are related structural results, not progress on the stated question, and carry no AI involvement. A 2021 paper (arXiv:2108.13834) and a 2019 paper (arXiv:1912.09290) proving conditional/special cases both predate the window. The one genuinely new and notable post-window event is Axiom Math's AxiomProver, an AI system, producing a machine-checked Lean 4 formalization (released 17 August 2026, conditional on the Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem) of the existing Maynard/Polymath8b argument for the 246 bound — described by the company and IEEE Spectrum coverage explicitly as a reconstruction/verification of a known proof, not a new mathematical result. Because this changes nothing a careful person would write in the conjecture's entry (no new n, no tightened bound, no case newly settled), and because the AI's role was formalization of an already-completed human proof, the record is classified status=open/no_change_found=true and ai_role=none per the formalisation_only rule (§6.2). Wikipedia's own article is unchanged and does not mention this formalization.
competing_reading: One could argue the Axiom Math formalization deserves a 'progress' or 'claimed' status as an instructive AI-related incident even though it doesn't move the mathematical needle, since it is the single most substantial thing that happened to this problem's surrounding literature in the window. But per §3.1 and §6.1, status must reflect the state of the conjecture as stated, and a formalization of a 12-year-old result changes nothing about what a careful person would write about Polignac's conjecture today; it is documented in ai/summary but does not justify moving status off 'open'.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or announcement that reduces the [2,246] bound further, proves the conjecture for a new specific even n via a genuinely new construction, or proves/disproves the general conjecture, dated after 26 January 2024.
